Title: The Regulation of Non-Scheduled Air Services in the United Kingdom 1960 to 1972
Abstract: THE Civil Aviation (Licensing) Act I960 established in the United Kingdom a system of licensing for the civil aviation industry. Among other measures, the Act created the Air Transport Licensing Board (A.T.L.B.) as a semijudicial tribunal to which United Kingdom airlines were bound to apply for licences to operate air services. Both the state-owned airlines, B.O.A.C. and B.E.A., and the private sector airlines thus required licences. During the course of the A.T.L.B.'s history (from I960 to I972 in effect) non-scheduled operations grew at an annual rate some three times faster than scheduled operations [i ]. A very large part of the non-scheduled operations came to be on behalf of tour operators offering inclusive tours (package holidays). During the period of rapid growth, the A.T.L.B. expressed concern at the effect of demand by tour operators on the non-scheduled airlines, in particular at the forcing down of the prices of charters for inclusive tours and at the financial instability which, it was argued, afflicted the non-scheduled airlines as a result. Concern was also expressed at the diminution of the consumer's choice of package holidays which might result from emergence of a few large firms of tour operators dominating the market. These fears were not allayed, despite the measures taken by the A.T.L.B., in part perhaps because it had no jurisdiction over the tour operators, who were merely the charterers of airline capacity. An examination of the A.T.L.B.'s policy and practice is of interest not only in the context of air travel and tourism but also in the context of transport regulation generally.

Title: An Index of Entry Barriers and its Application to the Market Structure Performance Relationship
Abstract: IN previous research (Orr, 1974) we estimated a model which expressed entry as a function of various incentives to enter and barriers to entry. From these basic empirical results, the present paper constructs an index of the overall level of entry barriers for each of the 71 Canadian three-digit manufacturing industries. This index, and its underlying methodology, should be more useful than any alternative empirical measure of overall entry barriers currently available. Unlike the classification scheme of Mann (Mann, I966), the weights attributed to the individual barriers in our index are empirically determined rather than subject to the authors judgment. Also, our index is continuous rather than discreet, and available for all (71) manufacturing industries rather than a small (30) selected sample. Some measure of the overall level of entry barriers is crucial to anti-trust investigators, as well as economists interested in the interaction between market structure and performance. Both Bain (1956) and Mann (I966) agreed that seller concentration alone is not an adequate indicator of monopoly power. They conclude that entry conditions are a crucial additional aspect of market structure. Accordingly, Part II identifies and ranks the manufacturing industries according to the level of entry barriers. This index of entry barriers is then employed to re-examine several issues current in the market structure-performance literature. As a first application (Part III) we examine the relationship between entry barriers and profitability in light of Mann's (I966) conclusions. The interaction between barriers and concentration on profits provides another application of our index (Part IV). After numerous attempts, this Rhoades (I97I, 1972) vs. Mann (I966, 1971, I973) debate seems unresolved. Thirdly, we examine the question, Do firms with a very high degree of monopoly power use this power to earn the higher profits predicted? Can we support the hypotheses that they restrain themselves to discourage entry or government regulation, or that monopoly power weakens the incentive for profit maximization?

Title: Optimization of Input Supply Patterns in the Case of Fuels for Electric Power Generation
Abstract: Procedures for procurement of coal and oil for electric power generating facilities are reviewed to provide data on contracting choices. Length of contracts and provisions for integrated fuel procurement are influenced by a variety of factors, including fuel substitution, future markets, and the size of fuel requirements. Suppliers need the security of long-term commitments with the provision for meeting increased costs, while buyers need the stability of quality control, regular deliveries, and protection from unanticipated price rises. Short-term methods, as in spot buying, introduce transportation costs, but offer flexibility to smaller operations. The basic problem is to insure that risks are fairly and actually reduced. Renegotiation provisions can be made to apply when either side feels the contract has become unfair. Tables provide data on the procurement of coal, based on size of requirement, percentage of total burn, and coal mining output. The role of alternative pricing methods and techniques of escalation of long-term contracts are analyzed in terms of percentage of industry burn. (DCK)

Title: Evaluating Scale Economies: The Case of Japanese Blast Furnaces
Barriers to Entry and the Stability of Market Structures: A Note
Abstract: PROFESSORS Bain and Mann were puzzled by one result of their investigation of the relationship between entry barriers and profitability. They expected, reasoning from the limit price theory,' to find significant differences among mean rates of return for their three classifications of entry barriers: very high, substantial, and moderate to low. Title: Some Observations on Exit from the Motor Insurance Industry, 1966-1972

In conlsequence a mass of literature has emerged;2 at different levels of sophistication each contribution purports to emphasize the importance of potential competition in influencing industrial behaviour-particularly in relation to pricing policies-and hence on performance, profits and industrial structure. In the meantime there has been little discussion of the opposite processof the causes and effects of exit on business behaviour and industrial structure. Of course, a large and growing literature on merger exists,3 and to that extent the effect of exit has been examined. Title: The U.K. Potato Crisp Industry, 1960-72: A Study of New Entry Competition
The Industrial Economics of Britain's Entry into the E.E.C.--A Framework for Analysing the Dynamic Effects
Abstract: IIN discussing the dynamic effects of E.E.C. entry on industry in Britain, the White Paper2 and pro-market economists have emphasized the benefits of a 'large and fast-growing home market'3 and the importance, in modern industry, of economies of scale.4 There is, however, a vital link which is missing in the argument: we seem to be left in the dark as to why actual membership of the Community is necessary for, and the precise mechanisms whereby it will lead to, the attainment of these benefits. Thus, the Six have had higher rates of economic growth than Britain, but why should entry be necessary for transmission of this growth? Is growth just like a contagious disease, and how will membership trigger the contagion? It is with these questions in mind that this paper has been written. The purpose of writing this article, however, is not so much to 'prove' that entry will automatically lead to beneficial dynamic effects, but rather to answer the question: if dynamic effects are to occur, in what possible ways will they occur? If anti-market economists should find my framework useful in showing that entry is bad for Britain, this paper will have achieved its aim. Until now the debate has been conducted too much like a 'dialogue of

Title: Business Pricing Policies in Japanese Manufacturing Industry
Abstract: THE purpose of this paper is to present some empirical evidence, for Japanese manufacturing industry, on several hypotheses concerning business pricing policies. We are interested in particular in the role demand factors play when prices are marked up over costs, and also in the so-called administrative inflation hypothesis that asserts that price increases are higher in more concentrated industries. The relation between price increases and concentration ratios was examined in a recent paper by Phlips.' Following Weiss' work2 which produced mixed results for the United States, Phlips found for Belgium, Netherlands and France that the effect of concentration on prices was either negative or zero, thus rejecting the administrative inflation hypothesis. It will be one of our findings in the present paper that this is also the case with Japan; neither output prices nor input prices (the meaning of which will be explained below) exhibit movements positively associated with concentration. Since Japan's is a fairly closed economy, the concentration ratios may safely be taken to measure monopoly power so as to make our test relevant, a point emphasized by Phlips. To single out the effect of concentration, it is of course necessary, as emphasized by Weiss, to introduce demand and cost factors in the analysis. As for costs, we have used a somewhat elaborate set of data which will be discussed below. The role of demand factors in the price equation of the cost-markup type will be interesting in its own right. Recently, Rushdy and Lund found, for British manufacturing industry, that the level of demand is a significant factor in the explanation of price changes.3 In studies of this kind the choice of a demand variable presents some difficulties.4 We have

Title: Prices and Profits in Petrochemicals: An Appraisal of Investment by Less Developed Countries
Authors: M. A. Adelman, Martin B. Zimmerman
Abstract: ALMOST every country with its own oil and gas production or a refining industry is investing in petrochemical production. This is increasingly true in less developed countries.' The petrochemical sector is considered a 'dynamic' one. Low prices are usually assumed to be temporary and due to excess capacity. This massive entry into an industry by capital-short countries calls for an analysis in the context of petrochemical industry behavior. We show why most LDC's will find success elusive, and why the best policy is non-entry.2

Title: Growth and Product Differentiability as Factors Influencing Changes in Concentration
Authors: James A. Dalton, Stephen A. Rhoades
Abstract: concentration reducing force because smaller firms and potential entrants are encouraged to expand (or enter) during rapid growth periods since they can do so without encroaching on the market of existing firms.' This hypothesis has been examined empirically but the results are conflicting.2 The second hypothesis is that concentration is more likely to increase or least likely to decrease in industries which produce differentiated goods.3 The rationale for this hypothesis is that in industries where product differentiation is important, a few firms tend to become favored over all others and are thereby enabled to maintain their market shares. Moreover, it is argued that due to risks associated with programs of product differentiation, there are likely to be dramatic rises by some firms and declines by others, and therefore, concentration is likely, ceteris paribus, to rise in these industries.4

Title: Advertising and Inter-Industry Competition: Testing a Galbraithian Hypothesis
Abstract: THE role of advertising as a competitive weapon within consumer goods industries has received considerable attention from empirical researchers in recent years. Studies have found generally that a firm's market share is related positively to its share of the industry's advertising.1 There is also some evidence of a ratchet effect at work in competitive advertising situations which causes an upward trend in advertising intensity over time in some industries.2 In The New Industrial State, Professor Galbraith has postulated that advertising is effective not only within a given industry, but is also effective in shifting customers between industries: 'If advertising affects the distribution of demand between sellers of a particular product, it must also be supposed that it affects distribution as between products.'3 The purpose of this paper is to examine the pattern of advertising expenditures in the U.S. consumer goods sector during the period 1948-67 and to perform an empirical test of Professor Galbraith's hypothesis.

Title: An Industrial Performance Evaluation Experiment
Employment and Output Functions for New Zealand Manufacturing Industries

Title: The Determinants of Pricing Behaviour: A Study of the Canadian Cotton Textile Industry
Market Structure and Economic Performance in U.K. Manufacturing Industry
Abstract: THERE is now a wealth of literature investigating the empirical relationships between various structural and behavioural characteristics of industries and their economic performance.1 The original objective of this work was to test the simple hypothesis that excessive market power, by removing the need to keep prices down to their competitive levels, enables firms to earn excessive profits. It was thought that the market power enjoyed by a firm depends on two factors, the degree of seller concentration in the industry it is operating in, and the height of barriers to entry into the market. The difficulty of entry was assumed to depend mainly on the importance of economies of scale, and the extent to which product differentiation is supported by high advertising expenditure. The relevant profit rate was taken to be either the rate of return on assets or the price-cost margin, and the degree of seller concentration was measured by the percentage of industry sales (or employment or assets) accounted for by a given number of the largest firms in the industry. Thus the hypothesis was normally tested by looking for a positive association between profit rates, averaged over the firms in each industry in a chosen sample of industries, and measures of the factors thought to determine market power; or alternatively, by looking for a positive relation between the profit rates of each firm in a chosen sample of firms, and the measures of market power. The results showed that there is indeed a positive correlation between concentration and profit rates, and entry barriers and profit rates, but the association was not strong and varied considerably according to the sample of industries chosen, the particular variables used, and the source of the data. No categorical statements about the relationships between market power and economic performance could be made on the basis of these studies. The importance of this work stems from the desire to base government policy towards the structure and behaviour of industry on a firm foundation of empirical knowledge. Public policy towards monopolies and mergers rests on the idea that increased seller concentration may lead to excess prices and

Title: The Fiscal Treatment of Shipping
Abstract: The article shows how the effects of fiscal and financial arrangements on the incentive to invest in ships can be calculated. The fiscal measures include corporation tax, investment grants, depreciation allowances and financing by retained profits and loan capital. Individual formulas are worked out and a variety of tables and graphs are prepared in the Appendix.

Title: Returns to Scale in Research in the Ethical Pharmaceutical Industry: Some Further Empirical Evidence
Abstract: performance. There is general agreement that competition between the makers of prescription (or ethical) medicines is conducted principally through the search for and marketing of new patentable products, price competition playing a relatively minor role. The international research-based companies, which occupy an important place in the ethical sector, typically spend 7-12% of their turnover on research and development1 (R and D), and worldwide research expenditure is currently of the order of f500 million per annum, of which some half is incurred in the United States and £25 million in the U.K. Recent years have witnessed a number of mergers in which the advantages of size in research activities have often been cited as a major inducement. The British industry, for example, has recently undergone a merger battle involving the Beecham Group, Glaxo Group and the Boots Company, which was eventually settled by a Monopolies Commission ruling that any merger would inhibit pharmaceutical research and innovation and so act contrary to the public interest. Against this background, the present paper focuses on output from the pharmaceutical innovation process and its relationship to research input and firm size. It mentions some problems arising in empirical work on this topic, with reference to previous studies. It presents new indicators of innovative output developed in a project carried out for the Chemicals Little Neddy2 and gives the results of statistical analysis based on these data.

Title: On the Rationality of Limit Pricing
Abstract: THE theory of limit pricing had its genesis in a suggestion of Harrod's (I952) that firms in monopolistically competitive markets might not reach the 'tangency solution' of Chamberlin (with its implied excess capacity) but might rather set a price lower than the tangency price, so as to discourage the entrance of new competitors.' This suggestion was later adopted by Bain (1956) and Sylos-Labini (I957) and made into the key feature of a theory of oligopoly price. The independent contributions of Bain and Sylos-Labini were reviewed, synthesized, and extended by Modigliani (i 958). The result promises to become a standard part of the apparatus which serves in place of a theory of oligopoly. It appears, for example, as a basic element in the recent study of Dewey's (i969) and is given more than passing attention by Scherer (1970). Moreover, the theory has recently been examined in a dynamic setting by Wenders (I97i) and Kamien and Schwartz (I97I). This dynamic extension is a perfectly natural development, as the problem of entry and what to do about it is, from the standpoint of established firms, inherently dynamic. Entry takes time. However, while it is true that a dynamic formulation is bound to be more satisfactory than a static one, a complete understanding of the theory's static properties is necessary for its proper development. This note is directed toward that end.

Title: The International Diffusion of an Innovation
Stock-Market Based Measures of Corporate Diversification
Abstract: INCREASED diversification is one step that many business firms take to reduce the probability of bankruptcy or ruin and to increase the efficiency with which internal resources may be allocated.' Accordingly, among the more interesting problems confronting researchers in the general area of corporate behavior is the measurement of corporate diversification for it at once involves analytic complexity and data inaccessibility. Concerning the former, it is difficult to choose between a diversification measure based on product diversity or one based on the number of distinct markets served; more pointedly, there is no physical measure of diversification which combines both. Regarding the other part of the problem, we note that sufficiently detailed data on any given firm's activities in the production and/or marketing areas are extremely difficult to obtain. This paper attempts to add some perspective to this problem by identifying an easily computed measure of diversification which, given the assumption of relatively perfect capital markets, contains elements of both product and market diversification. This paper is organized along the following lines. In Section II, the market model2 is introduced, briefly described, and shown to be applicable to the question of diversification measurement.3 In Section III, some commonly used physical measures of diversification are defined and detailed empirical results concerning the relationship of the measure suggested by the market model and physical measures are presented and discussed. Section IV concludes the paper.

Title: The Critical Level of Concentration: An Empirical Analysis
Authors: James W. Meehan, Thomas D. Duchesneau
Abstract: * The authors would like to thank H. Michael Mann, Robert W. Kilpatrick and John A. Preston, Concentration and Price-Cost Margins In Manufacturin,g Industries (Berkeley: University of California Press, I968), pp. I8-50. To our knowledge, there are approximately thirty such studies. Leonard Weiss in a recent paper, presented to a joint meeting of the American Economic Association and the Econometric Society, entitled 'Quantitative Studies of Industrial Organization' in Frontiers of Quantitative Economics, ed. by M. D. Intriligator (Amsterdam: North-Holland Publishing Co., 1971) pp. 362-403, provides an excellent critical analysis of these studies. 2 To our knowledge, there have been only two published studies, George Stigler's Capital and Rates of Return in Manufacturing Industries (Princeton: Princeton University Press, I963) and Yale Brozen's, 'Bain's Concentration and Rates of Return Revisited', The Jouirnal of Law and Economics (October 1971), pp. 35I-6I, that have found little or no statistical relationship between concentration and profitability. Robert Kilpatrick reports that Stigler's method of correcting for excessive salary withdrawal contains a statistical bias. When the bias is corrected for, a positive and significant relationship between concentration levels and profitability is uncovered. See Robert Kilpatrick, 'Stigler on the Relationship Between Industry Profit Rates and Market Concentration', The Journal of Political Economy (May/June I968), pp. 479-88. Brozen argues that the positive and significant statistical relationship reported in previous studies is the result of using small samples to test the hypothesis, i.e., small samples bias the findings. He found that when Bain's sample [Joe S. Bain, 'Relation of Profit Rate to Industry Concentration: American Manufacturing, 1936-I940', The Quarterly journal of Economics (August I}95I, pp. 293-324] is expanded from 42 to 78 industries for 1939 (75 for 1940) there is no relationship between concentration levels and profitability. Obviously, a larger sample is preferred to a smaller sample if other things are equal. However, it is not correct to state, as a general proposition, that '[t]he smaller the sample, the greater the sample bias'. See Yale Brozen, op. cit., p. 36I. As one commentator concluded: 'A larger sample is better than a small sample of data of equal quality, but a small sample of carefully compiled information is better than a large sample of inaccurate material.' See Daniel B. Suits, Statistics: An Introduction to Quantitative Econonmic Research (Chicago: Rand McNally & Co., 1963), p. 76. Casual observation indicates that Brozen may not have found a positive relationship because his larger sample contains a number of industries which do not correspond closely to theoretical definition of an industry, e.g., food preparation, not elsewhere classified. as was pointed out elsewhere: 'It seems obvious to us that adding more and more poorly corresponding industries to the sample is more and more akin to adding, as bona fide observations, numbers drawn from a table of random digits, making the null hypothesis more and more difficult to reject,' H. M. Mann, J. A. Henning, and J. W. Meehan, Jr., 'Statistical Testing in Industrial Economics: A Reply on Measurement Error and Sampling Procedure', The Journal of Industrial Economics (November i 969), p. I00.

Title: Profit Rates and Market Structure of Advertising Intensive Firms
Authors: John M. Vernon, Robert E. M. Nourse
Abstract: THE relationship of advertising to corporate profits has become an increasingly important topic to economists and others interested in public policy toward business. For example, the I969 report by the President's Cabinet Committee on Price Stability states that market concentration has risen 'sharply and presistently' in consumer goods industries, and that this 'reflects the advantages of large scale advertising and of product differentiation held by large enterprises'. Furthermore, the report continues: 'This increasing concentration suggests that there has been a growth in the discretionary pricing power of sellers in these industries' [3, p. 82]. Donald F. Turner, while Assistant Attorney General for Antitrust, indicated that he deemed it appropriate to impose limits on advertising and promotional expenditures by firms that have attained 'undue market power' [29, p. io]. Recently, the Federal Trade Commission has accused breakfast cereal manufacturers of illegal monopolization [2i]. A major basis for the charge is the FTC belief that high advertising expenditures by the companies create effective entry barriers.1 The belief that advertising creates effective entry barriers is based primarily upon a rather large number of statistical studies that have examined the correlation between industry advertising expenditures and concentration ratios [i, 8, 9, II, 1I2, I5, I6, I7, I8, 23, 26, 28] and between industry profit rates and industry advertising expenditures [4, 5, 6, 19, 24, 32]. Recently, several studies have been published that correlate firm profit rates with weighted average advertising expenditures of the industries in which the firms participate [Io, I4]. We would summarize the results of these studies as follows :2 (i) the existence of a statistically significant positive correlation between advertising and concentration remains an open question, (2) the correlation (after accounting for the effects of other market structure vari-

Title: Investment and Competition from Boom to Recession: A Case Study in the Processes of Competition--The Dry Cleaning Industry
An Analysis of Efficiency of Scale and Organizational Form in Commercial Banking
Authors: Lionel Kalish III, R. Alton Gilbert
Abstract: COST and output observations for a sample of banks are examined in this article to determine how the efficiency of banks is related to their size and organizational form. Three organizational forms are compared-unit banks, branch banks, and holding company subsidiaries. Knowledge about the ways in which size and organizational form affect bank efficiency is important because one objective of bank regulation is efficient production, and the policies of bank regulators influence the size and organizational form of banks. Regulatory decisions on chartering new banks and allowing bank mergers affect the size of banks through the effects of such decisions on the number of banks in individual bank markets. Regulatory decisions on establishing branch offices and acquiring banks through holding companies influence the organizational form of banks. The sample of banks used in this study consists of 898 commercial banks that participated in the Federal Reserve's Functional Cost Analysis Program in i968.1 The banks in the sample are grouped in Table I by amount of their assets and their organizational form. Banks of all three organizational forms are drawn from a wide range of asset sizes, with concentrations in the range from $io million to $50 million. Unit banks make up 5' per cent of the sample, 39 per cent of the banks are branch banks, and I o per cent are holding company subsidiaries.

Title: On Revenue Maximizing Duoply

Abstract: This paper examines the general factors which account for the differences between freight rates on commodities in shipping conference tariffs. The study gives special emphasis to the contributions of stowage factors, unit value and value of total trade in determining ocean liner freight rates.

Abstract: PROFESSOR Ross blames me for not having written a paper on the subject he is interested in (and working on). Faced with such a charge, the offender has an easy defence: it suffices generally to answer that one was doing what one was doing. However, Ross raises so many questions (some of which are interesting while others are wrong and/or unfair), that it is worth while to try to answer the more interesting ones. Furthermore, the problem Ross is interested in is important and worth investigating. In the second part of this reply I shall give a sketch of the paper I wish Ross had written to make his point.

Title: Illusions in Testing for Administered Prices
Abstract: PROFESSOR PHLIPS in this Journal (Vol. XVIII, November I969) has mounted what may be the latest foray against administered prices. Applying some routine statistical tests on data for Belgium, the Netherlands and France between 1958-65, Phlips concludes: 'Concentrated industries appear to behave in the same way as unconcentrated industries as far as upward flexibility is concerned. Prices tend to follow increases in unit costs, while market structure does not appear to have any particular influence' (p. I4). These remarks can be placed in a historical context: if 'downward flexibility' is substituted for 'upward flexibility' they would summarize what A. Neal found 30 years ago in his study of prices during the Great Depression in the United States.' Apparently, contemporary economics has rejected the hypothesis originated by Gardiner Means relating market power to relative prices for all time and place-the preand post-war generations and the U.S. and E.E.C. countries being a statistically huge sample. And yet, of late, the nemesis of stabilization policy in the U.S. and elsewhere has been the persistence of what was thought to be the incompatible evils of inflation and recession. Their protracted occurrence in the U.S. forced a reluctant government to embrace the last resort of wage and price controls, and of lesser impact, prompted critics to speculate on a permanent shift of the Phillips curve. What seemed to underlay the remarkable reversal of policy was the concession that the causes of inflation were resistant to conventional macroeconomic policies even at a social cost of over 6 per cent unemployment. Would such a concession have been as necessary if factor and product markets were broadly and reasonably competitive? The question invites an appraisal of Phlips' essay. It can be shown that Phlips' conclusions are biased in at least three distinct ways: a failure to consider relevant evidence and argument bearing on the nature of the hypothesis; a specification error in the tested equations; and an econometric procedure that

Title: Seasonal Fluctuations in the Motor Vehicle Industry: A Comment
Abstract: SEASONAL fluctuations in unemployment are generally considered to arise, in the main part, from variations in weather conditions and from movements in demand. A comparison of preand post-war patterns of seasonal variations in the motor industry reveals an interesting example of the influence of changes in production practices, allied to changes in the seasonal pattern of demand, both elements reflecting in part the lessening impact of the annual Motor Show. The statistics used in this discussion relate to unemployment in the city of Coventry, in which the prime influence upon trends in employment (and unemployment) is the motor industry. In I967, for instance, the motor vehicle industry, defined by minimum list heading 38I of the Standard Industrial Classification (C.S.O., I958) accounted for more than 40 per cent of manufacturing employment in the area. In the pre-war period, the percentage figure was considerably higher than this. It has been shown that movements in total unemployment in Coventry very closely reflect variations in the level of activity in the motor industry (see Smith, I 97 I), and it is these figures which are used in the following discussion. Figures I and 2 illustrate the seasonal pattern of unemployment in Coventry for the years I927-38 and I95I-69, respectively. The difference between the two diagrams is dramatic, displaying almost opposite trends. During the pre-war period, the seasonal 'peak' in unemployment tended to come in the summer months; in particular from June to August. This sort of pattern was likely to have been associated with the practice which car manufacturers made of spending the summer months in 'research and development', intent upon being able to produce new models in time for the Motor Show, which customarily took place in the autumn (see Turner, I963). During the I 930S, the car firms were numerous, but generally relatively small. This meant that resources were limited, so that 'research and development' and production could not be carried on simultaneously. However, in the years since the war, this situation has ceased to dominate. The car producers have grown in the scale of their activity, through mergers and in response to the large-scale expansion of demand. It is now possible, therefore, to carry out research and

Title: A Note on Variable Patent Life
Authors: Fred D. Arditti, Richard L. Sandor
Abstract: THE U.S. patent system seeks to stimulate inventive effort by offering the inventor the incentive of a seventeen-year right to exclusive use and by requiring public disclosure of the invention so that new knowledge is made available to other potential inventors. One distinct fact emerges from a study of this patent system: the seventeenyear life is not based on present-day economic phenomena but is somewhat of a historical accident.' This particular duration of exclusive use may not give the firm a large enough fraction of the social benefits associated with the invention to induce it to undertake a major R & D project involving a large investment. In this instance, society would forgo the benefits of the new product or process. On the other hand, a seventeen-year monopoly right might grant the firm a larger fraction of the ensuing social benefits than would be necessary to induce it to undertake a low cost R & D project. In this case, society would bear the social cost associated with an excessive patent life-a deadweight consumption loss.2 This reasoning leads one to suspect that there is no single patent life which might be deemed best. In spite of numerous examples in the literature which indicate the shortcomings of a fixed patent life in general, and a seventeen-year patent life in particular, there have been few real attempts to propose and analyze a system which would yield different patent lives for different inventions. It would seem that a system which advocates a variable patent life policy is one which should attempt to consider the alternatives of additional incentive versus the social cost of monopoly. It is the broad purpose of this paper to develop a system which does consider the preceding and to treat some of the difficulties associated with trying to determine patent life.

Title: Regulation, Profits and Entry in the Television Broadcasting Industry
Abstract: THE television broadcasting industry is similar to other oligopolistic industries in that in the absence of high barriers to entry, high profits among existing firms should cause new firms to enter the industry. On the other hand, it is different from oligopolistic manufacturing industries in that under current regulation by the Federal Communications Commission new firms can not enter any market without a license from the FCC and existing firms typically can not expand their quantity of output in response to rising demand. Once a television station is broadcasting the maximum number of hours per day and using a powerful transmitter to cover the largest area allowed in a particular market, it has no way to reach a larger potential audience. It can not legally build a second transmitter and simultaneously broadcast a second set of programs in the same market. On the other hand, of course, it can change the quality of its programs in order to attract a larger share of the available audience. Suppose we wish to predict whether a new station will enter a market where several stations are already broadcasting. One condition for new entry is that the potential station be able to obtain a license from the FCC. The lack of such a license is an absolute (legal) barrier to entry in any television market. This is an important consideration because the FCC determines in advance through an allocation table the maximum number of stations which shall be allowed in any market, and there are presently markets with no unused allocations available, and therefore no possibility of new entry into the market. Such markets include most of the largest io cities in the U.S. On the other hand, where barriers to entry are not too substantial, high profits should lead to new entry, particularly since existing firms can not increase the quantity of their output. A naive but still useful model of the broadcasting industry can be developed based on the assumption that each firm including any new entrant obtains an equal share of the market. Moreover, for the purpose of this model it is assumed that all firms have equal operating costs, viewing audience, revenue and profits. This model is naive because in reality in any market with four

Title: The Economic Significance of Small Firms
Abstract: A STEADY growth in the concentration of industry has been a feature of most advanced countries for about half a century. Economic theory attempts to explain this process in terms of technical, managerial, marketing and financial factors affecting existing firms and industries: little is said about the emergence and growth of new firms, and official statistics tell us very little about the smaller unquoted firms in the economy. It was partly to rectify this lack of information and partly because of concern expressed about pressures operating in a discriminating fashion against small firms, that a committee was established inJuly I969 to examine this sector. Under the chairmanship ofJohn Bolton, it produced its report' in November I97I. Its terms of reference were:

Title: In Defence of the Industrial Training Act

Industrial Electricity Consumption--An Example of an Intermediate Good
More on the Output Elasticity of Energy Consumption
Abstract: IN work published in I968, Adams and Miovic' noted that the output elasticity of energy consumption (commonly called the energy coefficient) was a somewhat amorphous parameter, differing substantially between countries and changing over time. They demonstrated that if energy statistics were adjusted to take account of the different efficiencies of the different main fuels the resulting adjusted energy elasticity was much more stable. Because of substitution of more efficient for less efficient fuels the unadjusted elasticity was often less than one in developed countries. The adjusted elasticities on the other hand lay between I.25 and I.4 when related to GDP and between I.04 and I.I5 when related to industrial production, the ranges in each case covering the different types of regression exercise by which the efficiency-in-use coefficients were computed. This paper develops a simple theory governing the relationship between useful energy consumption and national output that explains why the adjusted elasticities found by Adams and Miovic turned out to be greater than one. The theory is quantified by reference to a wide range of countries covering the whole spectrum of economic development and is tested against the actual experience over 20 to 25 years of individual countries. Conformity to the theory was very close and the efficiency-in-use coefficients computed by Adams and Miovic were found to hold good for periods of 20 to 25 years. Briefly, the hypothesis states that as a country moves through the various stages of its economic development from primitive subsistence agriculture to the ultimate state of fully energy-dependent2 production, its useful energy elasticity steadily falls froma high value (in principle, from infinity) tending asymptotically to one. This hypothesis follows directly from the fact that if a country is moving steadily towards a higher degree of energy-intensiveness in production then the specific energy content of incremental output will be higher than the average for all output, i.e.

Title: Some Preliminary Evidence of Imperfections in Markets
Authors: Richard W. Furst, Robert E. Markland

Title: Nonprice Competition in Jet Aircraft Capacity
Structure and Behavior in British Industries, with U.S. Comparisons
Abstract: THE basic questions about market structure concern what it is, what determines it, and what effects it has. Conceptual and econometric answers to the questions are still formative, even after three decades of research [2, IO, I8, 25, 29, 40]. Few hypotheses have acquired firm empirical support, and structure-performance relations in large areas of market activity remain conjectural. British industry is relatively unexplored, even after several pioneering efforts. Its patterns are of concern both for domestic industrial performance and as tests of hypotheses which are of more general interest and importance. This paper touches on both contexts. It first derives measures of British industrial market structure in recent years and uses them to indicate the extent of structural monopoly during 1958-63, in Section i. It next uses these measures in Section 2 to test hypotheses about comparative British and U.S. concentration. Section 3 then offers partial tests of two basic hypotheses about the determinants and effects of market structure: that growth erodes concentration over time, and that the degree of structural monopoly affects pricecost behavior. The findings conflict with several accepted conclusions and confirm several others, even though the data are imperfect and the period is brief and possibly atypical. Section 4 summarizes the findings.

Title: Changes in the Top 100 Quoted Manufacturing Companies in the United Kingdom 1948 to 1968
Company Pricing Policy
Economies of Scale in Retailing: A Note
Abstract: IN a recent article R. P. R. Tilley and R. Hicks' (hereafter referred to as T & H) examined the relationship between the size of supermarkets and various aspects of their operating performance. Although their article is entitled 'Economies of Scale in Supermarkets' there is in fact very little evidence which relates to this topic. Rather, they are concerned with more general relationships between size and performance. It is the purpose of this note to show that their analysis is not soundly based. As far as economies of scale are concerned it is necessary to ask two questions. Do economies of scale exist? If so, to what are they attributable ? In seeking to answer the first question a careful scrutiny of the data is necessary to reduce to a minimum the importance of any features which have differentially affected the basic information.2 Because all the supermarkets were controlled by a single company and there was a 'fairly uniform' pricing policy and no great variation in the quality of management, T & H state that it was possible to make meaningful comparisons between supermarkets. However, this is doubtful. Three factors may be mentioned which might well have a differential effect on the size-classes of supermarkets. 3 First, there are locational differences. T & H themselves point out that over half the supermarkets were situated in high streets, about a quarter were country branches and about a sixth were situated on estates. What relationship existed between these three types of location and size of supermarket.? It is likely that the larger supermarkets were concentrated in the high streets, with the estates and country regions having a high proportion of the smaller branches. Title: Raising the Capital Budgeting Hurdle
The Fixed Coefficients Production Process Under Production Uncertainty
Vertical Quasi-Integration
Heavy Commercial Vehicles: The Survival of the Small Firm
Abstract: IN the British car industry all the significant independent producers have been eliminated or absorbed by larger groups. The only independent survivors are those supplying the needs of customers with considerable financial resources, or with high performance and sporting requirements, or both. As cars are essentially a consumer good, 1 the survival of small firms in the car market depends upon the continued existence of consumers with needs and effective demands differing from those of the general mass of the motoring public. Even so the total production of the specialists2 is very small, accounting for o.52 per cent of the motor industry's total output in I969.

Title: Iron Ore and Steel: A Case Study of the Economic Causes and Consequences of Vertical Integration
Abstract: FUEL, water, and iron ore are the most important inputs used in the production of pig iron; pig iron is the most important input used in the production of steel. Because of the high transportation costs, before I830 American pig iron producers found it most profitable to locate where these three inputs existed in conjunction.1 At this time successful pig iron firms were small, sold their product in narrow geographical markets, and produced for their own use most of the necessary raw material inputs. After i 830, as anthracite coal became an economical fuel, as huge geographically concentrated deposits of iron ore were discovered and developed in areas far away from the nation's major population centers, and as the nation's internal transportation improved, sharply increased scale economies arose in the production of both of pig iron's principal mineral inputs. At the same time, the scale economics of pig iron production were increasing at a much slower rate. Thus, most successful pig iron producers began to realize diminishing profits in the production of both iron ore and fuel. Hence, they began to find that it was more profitable to buy both mineral inputs in the market. This realization led to a trend toward less backward integration by pig iron producers (and their successors, the crude steel producers) that continued unabated until the mid-I8gos. Between I896 and I900 more than two-thirds of the total iron ore consumed in the United States came from mines located in the Lake Superior region. In I896 more than one hundred companies were located in this region, and they produced 9,669,000 tons of iron ore. Twenty-six of these companies produced at least Ioo,ooo tons of iron ore and five produced more than 400,000 tons. The combined output of the five largest firms totalled 3,I30,000 tons and the largest (the Minnesota Iron Ore Company) produced almost goo,ooo tons. Authors: Morton I. Kamien, Nancy L. Schwartz

Title: Concentration, Barriers to Entry, and Long Run Economic Profit Margins
Public Responsibility in the Private Corporation
Abstract: FOR the past 40 years, the enterprise system serving as the engine of the American economy has been increasingly modified by a doctrine of social responsibility. By 'social responsibility' we mean voluntary restraint of short-term profit maximization. This restraint, not required by law, is purportedly exercised in the public interest. It reflects a judgment by the managers of a corporation that their powers are ultimately subject to public expectations that extend beyond the stockholders' interest in profit. The emerging doctrine recognizes that the 'invisible hand' of competition, postulated in the Wealth of J[ations as the ethical balance wheel preventing the selfseeking of men striving against each other from harming the public does not adequately check the power of great corporations capable of shaping their environments. A central assumption of this adaptation of economic theory is that regulation by government, while to some degree essential under imperfect competition, is not sufficiently knowledgeable, subtle, or effective to reconcile the self-interest of corporate entrepreneurship and the needs of a society being soretried as well as served by economic activity. I should like in this paper to acknowledge the difficulties of specifying precisely this theory of social responsibility, to assert nonetheless its powerful impact upon management behavior, to defend its validity as a partial substitute for increased regulation of private enterprise by the state, and to indicate how consideration of the public interest is brought into the strategic planning and policyformulation processes of the professionally managed corporation. The evolution of the American economic system, the security of the franchise granted by the American public to the private firm, the relationship between the individual and the company for which he works, and the very quality of national life will be crucially affected by the extension in practice of the concept of social responsibility. The subject is above all controversial. The American public is generating these days a passionate interest in consumer protection, rescue of the environment from pollution, and social justice. Even shareholder meetings are disturbed by insistence upon corporate involvement in these movements. Although the proponents do not command majorities in the voting of shares, they have alerted institutional holders of corporate securities, who own 40 per cent of securities listed on American exchanges, to the need to take stands.

Title: Market Structure and the Firm's Market Power
Abstract: In Economics there are certain notions which, though they provide a strong emotional appeal to public opinion, possess a very ambiguous scientific content. One such notion is the concept of "economic power". The gap between its apparent precision for the layman and its ambiguity for the economist is probably a reflection of the fact that the phenomenon is very deeply built into the economic system. It is thus quite difficult to obtain a clear and objective view of the reality of economic power. According to B. Russel, "the fundamental concept in social science is power, in the same sense in which energy is the fundamental concept in physics"

Title: Concentration and Specialization in Industry
The Large Firm in Modern Society
Cost Functions, Concentration and Barriers to Entry in Twenty-Nine Manufacturing Industries of India: A Reply
Long-Run Cost Curves: A Comment
Abstract: IN the November I 968 issue of this Journal, V. K. Gupta suggested a method of determining the long-run average cost (LAC) curve from essentially cross-sectional data. The annual Census of Indian Manufactures provides product value and total cost for plants classified according to industry and size of employment. The cost figure includes a depreciation allowance and appears to be total to the extent that the difference between product value and total cost is a 'before-interest-and-tax' profit margin. No allowance is made for a 'normal' rate of return on investment. Using the means of the five-year-average costs for the plants in each employment-size category, and using T for total cost (as defined in the Indian Census) and x for output, he wrote the LAC curve as T/x=f(x), i.e., the average cost is a function of output. 1 Three problems should be noted: (a) the extent to which the average rates of capacity utilization of the plants in each industry, are not at the points where their short-run average cost (SAC) curves are tangent to their respective LAC curves; (b) the bias2 created by averaging points lying on an SAC curve;' and (c) the effect of grouping the data.4 Mr. Gupta realizes the first and third, but does not appear to recognize the second, which will exist unless the curvature of eaclh SAC curve is zero.5 If, however, within each size category, the curvatures are small and of the same sign, the bias of the group will be small; and if the curvatures and ranges of plant operation are similar across categories, the group-bias may not vary with the plant-size category so that the position but not the shape of the LAC curve would be affected. He then uses cost divided by value of output as a measure of Tlx; employment as a surrogate for plant size (and thus as the independent variable); and estimates equations for twenty-nine Indian industries, selecting a 'best' equation in each case. These curves were then used to assess the extent of economies of scale in the industries.

Title: Cost Functions, Concentration, and Barriers to Entry in Twenty-Nine Manufacturing Industries of India: A Comment and Reinterpretation
Note On `The Determination of Selling Prices'
Abstract: In his paper 'The Determination of Selling Prices', [i] R. C. Skinner suggests that the most surprising aspect of accounting methods revealed by his survey of pricing procedures on Merseyside was the widespread use of variable costing [p. 21 i]. The firms were asked whether they had analysed their costs into fixed and variable elements, and if so, whether they normally made any use of the distinction in setting selling prices. Seventy-three per cent (I22 out of i66) of the respondents said they had made the distinction, and of these, 69 per cent used it in price-determination. Skinner points out that his findings on variable (or direct or marginal) costing are out of line with the results of other British investigations, which are described in a paper of mine [2]. He mentions a number of possible reasons for the discrepancy and concludes that the reason is more likely to lie in the nature of the question asked: 'A non-accounting manager may well not understand the meaning of such a question as Do you use marginal costing? Having never heard this description of the technique, he will probably reply No to the question [p. 2 I 2]. In fact, of the four investigations referred to in my paper, the questionnaires in Sizer's and Goodlad's [1] investigations were completed by accountants; Howe [4] visited the firms referred to in his investigations and interviewed the firms' accountants; and it is probable that accountants completed the questionnaires in the Hart & Prusmann [5] survey because of the technical nature of questions. In this note Skinner's interpretation of his results will be questioned.

Title: Snares in the Labour Productivity Measure of Efficiency: Some Examples from Indian Nitrogen Fertilizer Manufacture
Changes in the Size Structure of the Largest European Firms: An Entropy Measure
Abstract: While concentration ratios within particular industries are accepted as conventional indicators of market power, the use of an "overall concentration" approach has been viewed with suspicion. This approach defines overall concentration as being the proportion of some aggregate of economic activity accounted for by a relatively small number of the largest firms taken together.

Philip Andrews and Manufacturing Business
Philip Andrews and the Empirical Approach
Philip Andrews and the Oxford Economists' Research Group
Philip Andrews: Editor and Colleague
Abstract: IN the years before the war a great deal of empirical research was carried out at Oxford and Philip Andrews was very much associated with thc work that went on. It was felt that a new publication was needed, partly in order to present the results, and it was thus that Oxford Economic Papers came into being. Shortly after I arrived at Oxford as a ncwcomer in I946, it was decided that OEP should continuc. Hubert Henderson, Frank Burchardt and David Worswick became members of the new editorial board. I was invited to serve as General Editor and Philip became Secretary. Thus we began a close association which continued long after he left our board in order to found the new Journal of Induistrial Economics. The old OEP had been a collection of occasional papers which appeared at irregular intervals. We decided that the new series should be a journal and as time went on it began to attract an increasing flow of contributions from outside Oxford. There was a vast amount to be done. Philip's enthusiasm was unflagging and his energy inexhaustible. He was always full of ideas about the ways in which our policy should evolve and, at the same time, he was ready to devote unlimited effort to the exacting labour of producing the journal without the kind of secretarial assistance which would nowadays be taken for granted. Philip had a strong sense of continuity. He was anxious to ensure that the lines of research, both empirical and theoretical, with which he had been associated should be carried forward and he becamc the leading member of the Oxford Economists' Research Group. He was also concerned to ensure that the earlier contributions should be made more easily accessible, and it was thus that we came to edit together a book, Oxford Studies in the Price M/echanism, which contained reprints of some of the main articles from the old serics of Oxford Economic Papers together with some new essays. Over these years Philip was rapidly adding to his own understanding of industry and was developing what came to be known as the 'normal cost theory'. He had worked with the research group whose results were presented in the famous article by Robert Hall and Charles Hitch; but he saw clearly enough that this was only a starting point, though an important one. Some critically important questions had been left unanswered, and the theory of the kinked demand curve had not been adequately matched by the empirical findings. Philip soon began to push his own theoretical analysis well

Title: The Interaction of Barriers and Concentration: A Reply
Abstract: IN a recent paper,1 Stephen A. Rhoades claims to have found that barriers to entry have no significant influence on profitability independent of concentration. Rhoades goes so far as to state that '. . . the relationship between the rate of return [and concentration] in high barrier industries is not significantly different from rates of return in low barrier industries.'2 However, it will be shown that Rhoades' apparent finding is based entirely on an outright statistical mistake: the illegitimate pooling of observations from the high and substantial barrier classes. Rhoades established two barrier classes from the three reported in my earlier paper.3 My high and substantial barrier classes were combined into a single category, high barriers. The moderate-to-low barrier group remained as originally presented. Rhoades fails to investigate whether it is or is not statistically justifiable to combine the high and substantial barrier classes. The standard statistical test for combining observations is the Chow test.4 Rhoades' data, presented in Appendix Table A of his paper, yield the following four linear regressions of the relationship between profitability and concentration: equation (i) estimates the relationship for all 23 observations; equations (2), (3), and (4) estimate the same relationship for each barrier of my original three classes: high (2), substantial (3), and moderate-to-low (4). Standard errors are in the parentheses.

Title: Labor Demand, and Multi-Product Cost in Semi-Continuous and Multi-Process Facilities
Concentration, Promotion, and Market Share Stability in the Pharmaceutical Industry
Abstract: THE literature of economics includes many studies that attempt to determine relations among concentration, advertising, new product innovation, and the stability of market shares. Many hypotheses have been tested, but few unambiguous results have emerged. For example, the November, I 969, issue of the Journal of Industrial Economics contains the most recent in a series of exchanges among economists on the existence of a correlation between advertising and concentration. Lester Telser finds no relation in his work, while H. M. Mann, J. A. Henning, and J. W. Meehan, Jr., report statistically significant positive relations. Although a detailed discussion of the reasons for the different results is beyond the scope of the present paper, the type and quality of data used in the studies is a major source of dispute. Most of the studies have used publicly available data that are highly aggregated and that cover a large number of diverse industries. In view of the differences in results that have been obtained, it should be useful to test the hypotheses on new data whenever possible. Hence, in this paper we shall report some results for data covering i8 'therapeutic markets' within the United States ethical pharmaceutical industry. In almost all past studies, differences among industries other than advertising could have significantly affected the regressions of concentration on advertising. Hence, one advantage of this study is that by comparing similar therapeutic markets within a single industry we tend to control for the effect of these other factors. Of course, by the same token, our results are less general since they are based on a single industry. The paper is divided into five parts. In Part I we describe the characteristics of the data, define the variables, and provide an initial overview of the relations to be tested. Part II discusses the results obtained for the concentration equation, Part III is concerned with the promotion equation, and Part IV is devoted to the market share instability equation. The conclusions of the study are given in Part V.

Title: African Businessmen in a Dual Economy
Abstract: IN a society with marked cultural divisions, these divisions tend to intrude into economic life A racial or religious group dominates in one field of economic activity, while it is virtually excluded elsewhere. This is no accident, for the cultural bond can help to secure the social networks which carry business forward. But these cultural divisions also act as formidable barriers to change, cramping and distorting the evolution of new patterns of relationship. Economic innovation may then be stultified less by lack of resources than by lack of a social network, of conventions of mutual trust and understanding, through which to organize its affairs. This is a characteristic problem of a dual economy-meaning here simply any economy where such cultural divisions have become a dominant organizing principle of economic management. In this paper, I want to discuss the dual economy from the standpoint of a local businessman-not the manager, of an international company, nor the influential politician who sits on boards of directors, but the man who has built up his own concern, and is trying to be more than just a petty shopkeeper or a self-employed craftsman. Such a man stands in the middle of the systems of relationship in which the economy is divided. He is ambitious, progressive, yet still partly held by the values and obligations of the small-scale rural community in which he grew up. He has to think out afresh how to handle his suppliers, his bank, his workers and customers, because he is a newcomer to the commercial or industrial activity he undertakes and there are no precedents to guide him. Men of other races may have run similar businesses before, even in the same place, but they worked within the conventions of different cultures. He has to pioneer his own solution to the problems of management which confront him, mediating between the demands of economy institutions at large and the expectations of his own people. For him, the disjointedness of a dual economy presents a set of practical difficulties which he must overcome if his business is to survive. I will try to describe how African businessmen in Kenya characteristically handle this situation. My information comes mostly from

Title: On Suboptimization in Decomposition Approaches to Transfer Pricing
Authors: Philippe A. Naert, Christian T. L. Janssen

Title: Product Differentiation and Concentration in the Brewing Industry
Abstract: RECENT events in the American brewing industry should be of great interest to students of industrial economics. A spirited debate over the potentially anticompetitive effects of advertising has enlivened the literature in that field. At the same time the brewing industry has experienced substantial concurrent increases in market concentration and promotional expenditure.' It is natural to consider to what extent the two latter developments have been causally related. In two recent articles published in this journal, Ann and Ira Horowitz have presented an extensive description of the concentration trend in this industry, but with little more than a passing reference to the possible influence of advertising and other forms of product differentiation.2 It is the purpose of this paper to fill that void. The first section below contains a brief review of the rising concentration in brewing. The second section attempts to explain that trend, focussing particularly on the role of product differentiation. Economies of scale in production, another possible cause, are briefly explored in the third section, which includes a brief summary and statement of conclusions.

Title: An International Comparison of the Intranational Effects of Concentration on Industry Wages, Investment, and Sales
Economies of Scale for Machine Tool Production
Competition and Structural Change in Unconcentrated Industries
Abstract: COMPETITION owes its important place in economic theory to its presumed role in bringing about an efficient allocation of resources. Most economists would share a concern about a possible absence of competition, particularly in large-scale concentrated industries which are predicted by economic theory to be marked by a lack of interfirm rivalry; this concern has stimulated considerable research into the effect of concentration on performance. Much less has been written about a possible excess of competition in industries whose structure is likely to promote intense rivalry, namely, small-scale unconcentrated industries. Even the strong proponents of state intervention to promote competition would be unwilling to assert that there is a straightforward, monotonically increasing relationship between the intensity of competition and the promotion of the public interest and might well consider that the businessman's dislike of 'excessive' competition contains much economic sense.2 This paper draws attention to the role played by competition in changing industrial structures and questions the traditional assumption of economic theory that competition can be relied upon to bring about an optimal allocation of resources by the elimination of inefficient size-classes of firm and the promotion of the efficient. Our emphasis differs from that of Weiss3 who, in his study on the factors influencing changes in concentration, was concerned with the effects of the relatively high risks associated with product differentiation. The emphasis here is less on the type than on the intensity of competition. This enquiry also raises a related question which has some importance both in regard to the measurement of economies of scale and for policies aimed at providing assistance to small firms. Title: Concentration and Mobility: Alternative Measures of Industry Structure
Authors: Stanley E. Boyle, Robert L. Sorensen
Abstract: FOR the past 40 years, economists have relied upon concentration, however measured, as a primary description of industry structure. From time to time, complaints have been raised citing the technical shortcomings of this measure. Most of these suggestions have referred to the appropriateness of either (i) the variables used, or (2) the method of measurement selected. Throughout this period of time however, little if anything was done to develop other measures of structure which lend themselves to quantitative analysis. There are some exceptions to this, of course. Professor Bain attempted to appraise the impact of product differentiation upon industry performance.' More recently, the work of Mann, Telser and others has offered some hope that this approach may be more fruitful.2 A recent paper by Boyle and McKnew attempted to relate the level of product differentiation to both the magnitude and frequency of price changes in highly concentrated industries.3 One result of that study was to cast serious doubt upon the implicit, and sometimes explicit, assumption that product differentiation activities (most usually advertising) and price competition are necessarily substitutes for one another, i.e., that degree of product differentiation and price flexibility are inversely correlated. Interesting as they are, these studies do not assist materially in the analysis of the physical characteristics of a market. A major exception to this has come in the form of a limited number of studies which have attempted to provide an alternative analytical approach to the measurement of industry structure. These studies have attempted to describe, and to provide an analysis of, the significance of changes in the relative rankings of firms within some market through time. As Kaplan pointed out:

Title: A Note on Mergers and the Business Cycle: Comment
Concentration, Barriers and Rates of Return: A Note
Inter-Firm Production Function Analysis of Yugoslav Industrial Resource Allocation
Abstract: THE usefulness of empirical production functions is often limited by the poor quality or aggregate nature of the data from which they are estimated. The present study utilizes Yugoslav enterprise data of uniform high quality to estimate production functions which are then used to estimate a Pareto optimal pattern of capital and labor allocation. The criterion used for discriminating among all Pareto solutions is to choose the solution which will save the maximum amount of industrial capital yet produce the same level and composition of industrial output with the same total level of manhours.

Title: Diffusion of Catalytic Techniques Through a Population of Medium Size Petroleum Refining Firms
Abstract: THIS paper reports a study of the diffusion of two catalytic refining techniques, reforming and cracking, among forty-three medium-size petroleum refining firms. The paper has four parts: a brief description of the relevant technology; a development of some hypotheses; a report of research design and findings; a brief. interpretation of these findings. Petroleum is a mixture of compounds with different boiling points and molecular structures. Refining consists in separating the compounds and converting the less valuable compounds to higher valued compounds by changing their boiling points and/or structure. The most important product of petroleum refining is gasoline.1 '[T]he principal mark of gasoline quality has been resistance to knocking, which is expressed as number ' [Hengstebeck, 1959, P. 3]. In I950 the two main ways of converting petroleum compounds were cracking and reforming. Cracking does three things: breaks up large molecules into smaller ones; changes structures of molecules, most importantly increasing octanes of compounds in the gasoline boiling point range; recombines fragments into unwanted low value heavy compounds. Reforming compounds already in the gasoline boiling point range primarily changes their structure to increase octane without changing their weight. Although there is wide variation among petroleums, and the proportions devoted to various uses depends on market conditions, it is possible to make a rough * The theory that underlies the paper was developed jointly with Kenneth D. Mackenzie. Any error in applying the theory is mine. Nancy Bernhardt pointed out a logical error in an early draft and made extensive editorial improvements. Helpful comments were made by Frank Carmone, Irwin Feller, and W. Robert Needham. Many refining company executives generously gave time to fill out a questionnaire. 1 In I947, the nearest census date before the period studied, gasoline accounted for about 45 per cent of the value of petroleum refinery output [Cassady, 1954, p. io]. For plants with cracking facilities the proportion of value accounted for by gasoline tended to be higher-from approximately 60 per cent to over 75 per cent. This is based on statements of operating results for two hypothetical refineries with cracking equipment that appeared in trade journals. The 60 per cent figure assumes that market conditions favored 'limited gasoline and maximum kerosene and fuel oil production' [Read, 1946, p. 248]. The 75 per cent figure assumes that conditions favored the production of gasoline [Anon, 1949, p. 557].

Title: Some Problems Associated with the Marketing of Ethical Pharmaceutical Products
Abstract: ADVERTFISING frequently generates controversy. Few industries, however, have so much strong feeling aroused by their promotional activities as pharmaceuticals.' This paper discusses some of the specific reasons why pharmaceutical promotion may provide cause for concern and tries by statistical investigation to establish whether or not grounds exist for some of the criticisms to which the industry has been subjected. The paper is in two main sections. Firstly, promotion in the industry and some of the specific arguments which are directed against it are examined. Secondly, the variables used in a crosssectional, multiple regression analysis carried out on pharmaceutical promotion are described and the results of the analysis presented. The exercise was carried out using promotional data for the calendar year I966.

Title: Differences Among Cities, Differences Among Firms, and Costs of Urban Bus Transport
Abstract: This article explores the relationship between transit operating costs, characteristics of the firm and the environmental setting in which the firm operates. Data for analysis were obtained for thirty-three U.S. cities from the American Transit Association, National City Bus Lines and the Amalgamated Transit Union for calendar year 1963. Using cost per vehicle mile as the dependent variable, the author found operating costs to be higher for lower system speeds, older cities, and less intense route structures. Since route intensity and age were found to be inversely related, cost savings from a more compact route structure were cancelled out by the increased costs of congestion in older cities. The author concludes that the environment plays a significant role in explaining transit operating costs, particularly through the schedule speed variable, and that city descriptor variables should be considered in comparative analysis of urban transit performance.
